reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: Occurs almost exclusively in women of reproductive age, either sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis complex
Typically presents with progressive breathlessness, recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax, or chylous pleural effusions
High-resolution CT shows numerous thin-walled cysts distributed diffusely and uniformly throughout both lungs, in contrast to the upper-zone predominance of other cystic diseases
Extrapulmonary features include renal angiomyolipomas and lymphangioleiomyomas (abdominal or pelvic lymphatic masses)
A markedly elevated serum VEGF-D supports the diagnosis and can help avoid lung biopsy in the right clinical context
The abnormal smooth-muscle-like cells carry mutations in the TSC genes with resulting activation of the mTOR pathway, which is the rationale for mTOR inhibitor therapy
Sirolimus (an mTOR inhibitor) is used to stabilise lung function in patients with declining spirometry or problematic chylous effusions
Oestrogen appears to drive disease, so exogenous oestrogen and pregnancy may accelerate progression
reference.pathophysiology: LAM is characterised by proliferation of abnormal smooth-muscle-like cells (LAM cells) around airways, blood vessels, and lymphatics, together with diffuse cystic destruction of the lung parenchyma. The LAM cells harbour inactivating mutations in the tuberous sclerosis genes TSC1 or TSC2, leading to constitutive activation of the mTOR signalling pathway and unregulated cellular growth and migration. Cystic airway obstruction predisposes to air trapping and pneumothorax, while lymphatic involvement produces chylous effusions and lymphangioleiomyomas. The strong female predominance and hormonal sensitivity implicate oestrogen in disease progression.
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest to demonstrate diffuse thin-walled cysts
Abdominal and pelvic imaging for angiomyolipomas and lymphangioleiomyomas
Pulmonary function testing, typically showing obstruction with reduced diffusing capacity
Screening for tuberous sclerosis complex features
Lung biopsy reserved for cases that remain diagnostically uncertain
redFlags: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness indicating spontaneous pneumothorax, which may be recurrent
Large chylous pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise
Acute flank pain or haemorrhage from a bleeding renal angiomyolipoma
Rapid decline in lung function signalling progressive respiratory failure
reference.prognosis: Disease course is variable but generally slowly progressive; mTOR inhibitor therapy can stabilise lung function, and although some patients eventually develop respiratory failure requiring lung transplantation, overall survival has improved substantially with modern treatment.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in a young woman presenting with recurrent pneumothorax
Misclassifying the diffuse cysts as emphysema in a non-smoker
Failing to screen for renal angiomyolipomas, which can bleed
Not counselling against oestrogen-containing therapy and about pregnancy-related risk
